adds.title: Colorado Supreme Court sides with transgender youth in fight against Children's Hospital Colorado
adds.summary: The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on May 18, 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated the state's anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume the care (puberty blockers, hormone therapy). Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity'; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system. The ruling documents Colorado's highest court actively enforcing the gender-identity protections on which this record's anti-discrimination claim rests.

adds.title: Colorado voters will decide whether to ban trans kids from gendered sports, outlaw gender-affirming surgery for children
adds.summary: Colorado voters will decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender kids from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after state elections officials certified the voter signatures on the three measures including Initiative 108 on child sex trafficking (The Colorado Sun, Mar. 17, 2026). The initiatives were pushed by conservative activists and would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into state law. They are the first statewide ballot-level counter-pressure to Colorado's protective legal posture that this record documents.

adds.title: Colorado to suspend Medicaid coverage for some gender-affirming care for youth due to new federal rule
adds.summary: Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning Oct. 13, 2026, because a new federal rule finalized in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care for people under 18 (and under 19 under the CHP+ child program); the state's Medicaid agency said resuming coverage 'will require legislative action' (The Colorado Sun, Aug. 21, 2026). About 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, and patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period while behavioural healthcare is unaffected. The suspension shows Colorado's protections operating under direct federal-funding pressure, relevant to a trans visitor's assessment of the state.

adds.title: Era giusto rimuovere i manifesti di Pro Vita, i giudici danno ragione al Comune di Roma
adds.summary: On August 30, 2025 Rome's municipal administration announced that the Consiglio di Stato (the country's highest administrative court, seated in Rome) had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking 'gender' ideology in schools, on the ground that the images — one showing a boy being given a red hairbow — were discriminatory and that public spaces may not be used for messages that 'generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance', particularly concerning minors. The anti-trans campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The ruling is a dated judicial outcome in the region's largest city confirming that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted there, an institutional datapoint for this region record, which otherwise centres on violence statistics and the transphobic-motive verdict in Perugia.

adds.title: Morte di Samuele De Paoli, la Cassazione conferma l'assoluzione della trans Patrizia
adds.summary: On March 5, 2026 the Court of Cassation confirmed the appeal-court acquittal of trans woman Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson ('Patrizia') over the April 27, 2021 death of Samuele De Paoli in Perugia, finding the death was caused by cardiac arrhythmia from accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the charge of homicide final. The case, in this region's main university city, was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant. For this record it documents that the region's courts and the highest ordinary court decided a high-profile trans-related case on the facts, complementing the record's claim about judicial responses to transphobic violence.

adds.title: Saskatchewan Appeal Court says challenge of province's pronoun law can continue
adds.summary: The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that (LGBTQ+ group) UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years. This mainstream coverage independently traces the record's claim that the appeal court largely allowed the government's appeal while keeping the merits challenge alive.

adds.title: Amnesty International Canada welcomes ruling in court challenge to Saskatchewan pronoun law
adds.summary: Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The piece corroborates the durable signal this record draws from the case: a consent and name-change rule for transgender pupils shielded from ordinary rights review while litigation continues.

adds.title: Supreme Court to weigh in on Saskatchewan's school pronoun case
adds.summary: On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause (a five-year override). Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The grant is the key later development for this record: no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

adds.title: Kalinga (province) - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's article on Kalinga, a landlocked province within the Cordillera Administrative Region whose capital Tabuk was established when it was formed out of Kalinga-Apayao on 8 May 1995 by Republic Act No. 7878, documents the province as a long-standing flashpoint between the Marcos martial-law government (declared September 1972) and its indigenous peoples over the Chico River Dam Project, which would have displaced about 100,000 indigenous people, with the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turning public opinion and making the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case study in the country. It records the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord that created the Cordillera Autonomous Region and notes that attempts to ratify actual autonomy failed in plebiscites. For this record it frames the province's indigenous governance context in which the customary bodong/pagta justice system the summary concerns operates; it does not itself discuss the bodong/pagta codification.

adds.title: Cordillera Administrative Region - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's region framework page for the jurisdiction itself: the Cordillera Administrative Region was created on 15 July 1987, comprises six provinces (Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province) centred on Baguio, is the country's only landlocked region and, per the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, the least populated in the country with fewer residents than the national capital. It describes the region as home to numerous ethnic groups, including a majority-Igorot province, and records a living Cordillera autonomy movement alongside the earlier Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire secured by the Aquino government. A framework document for the jurisdiction in which the record's customary-justice claims sit, with the region itself as the subject.

adds.title: Daegu Queer Culture Festival - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's article on the Daegu Queer Culture Festival (DQCF), the festival at the centre of this record: it has been held every year since 2009 as the country's second-largest LGBT event, a pride parade and film festival lasting a week or two and usually taking place in late June, and it faces standing opposition from religious groups, with an estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups forming a 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu to block LGBT events. The page records that such opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street, and it carries survey context on national attitudes (Pew Research Center: 18% of South Koreans felt homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013). Framework source confirming the record's claim of an annual festival since 2009 and a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation in Daegu.

adds.title: Anti-queer groups file human rights petition over Daegu Queer Festival, countering the festival organizers - NOCUTNEWS
adds.summary: No Cut News (English, 8 June 2026): the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters — comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association — filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea (NHRCK) demanding a change of venue for the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, claiming the event is likely to infringe on public welfare; the group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single NHRCK petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Daegu's Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It counteracts the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Dated court-and-petition evidence that official venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation over the festival continued into the 2026 edition, directly supporting this record's account of a confrontational environment around the event.
